reason: The Commission found that EU citizens had no access to posts in public administration bodies in the 2023 report and the 2023 analytical report, and repeated the finding unchanged in the 2024 and 2025 reports. The 2026 report records that new legislation opened certain technical, specialised and auxiliary posts to EU citizens while civil servant posts remain reserved to nationals, so the improvement is legal only and partial.

Government Decision No. 566/2025 opens technical, specialist and auxiliary posts to persons without Moldovan citizenship, which the Commission confirms in 2026, and the Government plans an analysis, in the light of case law of the Court of Justice, of which civil service functions can be opened; its own account still excludes public functions that expressly require citizenship. What remains is opening civil servant posts to EU citizens, except those that involve the exercise of public authority and safeguarding the general interests of the State.

The finding is repeated in the 2023, 2024, 2025 and 2026 reports and concerns a core rule of the chapter, but it sits in the body text and no key recommendation, benchmark or Reform Agenda payment condition names it among the 10 Moldova items on this issue. Partial legal progress is recorded in 2026, so the route to High for a core requirement with no progress does not apply.

The change is a national legal matter with no dependence on other states, and the 2025 Government decision shows that categories of posts can be opened. The remaining step needs a review of civil service functions against case law, which the Government has so far only planned.

The 2023 analytical report found that national law covers most branches of social security but not pre-retirement benefits, gives no unemployment benefit to non-nationals with temporary residence, and needs capacity building in coordination. The 2026 report records the adoption of a law setting a legal basis for applying the coordination rules but does not assess its alignment, and its key recommendation asks for gap analyses of the coordination regulations, so no change in the Commission's assessment is shown. The Chapter 2 rating rose from an early stage in 2023 and 2024 to between some and a moderate level of preparation in 2026, but the progress it cites concerns bilateral agreements and EURES, so the scale was not decisive.

A law establishing the legal basis for applying the EU coordination rules and EESSI interconnection has been adopted, which is a legal step only, while the draft law on keeping unemployment benefit when moving and on frontier workers remains a proposal, and the Government states that current law does not regulate these cases; only 3 of 8 planned staff of the legal directorate work on harmonisation with European rules. What remains is a gap analysis and full alignment of national pension, health, unemployment and other social security law with Regulations (EC) No 883/2004 and No 987/2009, together with the administrative measures to apply them at accession.

Alignment with the coordination regulations is core acquis for the chapter, and the 2026 key recommendation asks for gap analyses of them. Among the 55 Moldova items on this issue, however, the requirement appears only in the 2023 analytical report and the 2026 report, not in a key recommendation repeated across three reports, a benchmark or a Reform Agenda payment condition.

The legal changes are within national control: a coordination law has been adopted and a detailed draft on unemployment benefits prepared. Against that, the work spans several institutions and benefit systems, specialist staff are few and the draft ties key provisions to the date of accession.

The 2023 analytical report found that authorities struggle with administrative capacity and data exchange in international cases, and the 2025 key recommendation asked Moldova to develop IT infrastructure for EESSI. In 2026 the Commission reports that the e-Governance Agency was designated as the EESSI National Access Point with two liaison bodies, a law setting the basis for EESSI interconnection was adopted and an EESSI Action Plan approved, while the 2026 key recommendation still asks for the IT infrastructure and capacity. The improvement is organisational and legal only, as no technical connection is reported.

The access point, liaison bodies, legal basis and action plan are in place, but the Government reports that the employment agency and CNAS systems still need adjusting for EESSI, that the technical solution and its financing will be chosen later, and that only 3 of 8 planned IT directorate staff work on the health insurance card and interconnection with European systems. What remains is the IT infrastructure, interconnected information systems, staff and funding for full participation in EESSI and for electronic exchange of health insurance data.

Electronic exchange is needed to apply social security coordination at accession, and it is named in the key recommendations of the 2025 and 2026 reports. Among the 31 Moldova items on this issue it does not appear in a key recommendation repeated across three reports, a benchmark or a Reform Agenda payment condition.

The 2026 designations and action plan show that organisational steps can be taken, and the Government reports the interoperability platform as technically ready for cross-border exchange. Connection, however, depends on technical documentation from the Commission, an investment not yet decided, several institutions and a new employment agency system funded externally.

The issue is not raised in EU material: the only Moldova item on it is the employment agency's own report of internal audit missions, one of them on how the EURES network is being implemented. A single item gives no sequence over time.

No item among the 1 Moldova item on this issue states an EU requirement on corruption prevention in the administration of worker mobility, and the audit report says nothing on integrity policy or internal controls. What remains is unknown, since no source states a requirement or a problem for Moldova on this issue.

The issue is not raised in EU material, as no item among the 1 Moldova item on it is from an EU source, which keeps priority from being High. The single item reports audit activity and does not describe a problem.

The one item shows that the employment agency has an internal audit service that carried out five assurance missions, but it gives no evidence on the actors, mechanisms or past progress needed to judge how tractable corruption prevention is.

The issue is not raised in EU material: no item among the 5 Moldova items on it is from an EU source. It first appears in the Government's 2025 accession programme, which plans Romanian courses for EU citizens, their family members and their children, so there is no earlier item from which to judge a trend.

All the measures are proposals: Romanian courses in schools and through the national programme for learning Romanian, a new programme for 2026 to 2028 with study centres, and a mechanism to pay teachers, and the Government says these could need additional teaching posts. What remains is, on the Government's own account, putting in place and resourcing host-language tuition for EU workers, their family members and their children.

The issue is not raised in EU material, which keeps priority from being High, and it rests on 5 Government items describing planned measures. Host-language tuition is a narrow strand of the chapter compared with access to employment and social security coordination.

Delivery rests mainly with the Ministry of Education and Research and builds on an existing national programme for learning Romanian. However, the new programme was still to be drafted in 2025, and teacher payment and any extra posts are not funded in the evidence.

The 2023 key recommendation asked Moldova to adopt the Digital Transformation Strategy 2023-2030 and ensure capacity to implement it; the strategy was adopted in September 2023 and a National Council for Digital Transformation set up in November 2023, as the 2024 report records. The 2025 report notes an implementation programme for 2025 to 2027 and tangible progress on all key performance indicators, and the 2026 report again records progress on them. The Chapter 10 rating rose from some level of preparation in 2023 to 2025 to moderately prepared in 2026, but it rates the whole chapter and was not decisive.

The strategy, the council and an implementation programme are in place, but the Commission repeats in 2024, 2025 and 2026 its key recommendation to ensure institutional capacity to implement the strategy. The Government reports 225 million lei of the programme's cost as uncovered, the ministry and the e-Governance Agency responsible for 53 and 37 of its 68 actions, and a lack of centralised coordination, and a 2024 follow-up audit by the Court of Accounts found its recommendations on IT governance only partly implemented. What remains is the staff, funding and coordination capacity in the ministry and the e-Governance Agency to deliver and monitor the strategy.

A key recommendation on adopting the strategy and ensuring the institutional capacity to implement it appears in the 2023, 2024, 2025 and 2026 reports, and strategy and governance are central to the digital transformation theme. The later recommendations name data protection and cybersecurity as the main areas for that capacity, which are covered by other issues.

The Government adopted the strategy, set up the council and approved the implementation programme within two years, and the Commission records progress on its indicators. Capacity is the harder part: the Government and the Court of Accounts report staff shortages, low pay for IT staff, staff turnover after reorganisations and reliance on external partners for funding.

The 2023 and 2024 reports find that the tax administration improved its electronic services, and the 2025 and 2026 reports record good progress in Chapter 16 that includes the digitalisation of tax administration services. The 2026 report still finds it essential to digitalise tax services further. The Chapter 16 statements cover the whole chapter, so the issue's own items were decisive.

The Reform Agenda sets a target of 18 of 19 taxpayer services digitalised by December 2026 and the 2026 report asks for further digitalisation, while the Government's indicator gives 64% of companies using e-invoices against a target above 70%. SIGMA found that only 10% of citizens filed personal income tax returns electronically for 2022, and the Reform Agenda names limited staff and taxpayers' preference for in-person services as barriers. What remains is completing the digitalisation of taxpayer services and raising their use, especially by citizens.

The digitalisation of taxpayer services is a Reform Agenda payment condition due by December 2026 and is repeated in the 2026 report, but it is a narrow strand of digital government on which the Commission records good progress in 2025 and 2026. No key recommendation names it among the 20 Moldova items on this issue.

The work lies with one agency, the Reform Agenda sets yearly targets with payments attached, and the Commission records improvement in every report from 2023 to 2026. Uptake depends partly on taxpayers' habits, which the Reform Agenda names as a barrier.

The 2023 report found limited progress on an e-health legal framework and no e-health strategy, and the 2024 report found no integrated health information system, although electronic prescriptions had operated since April 2024. The Reform Agenda in 2025 still notes no approved eHealth strategy or regulatory framework, and the 2026 report records the adoption of the National Programme for Digitalisation and Innovation in Health 2025-2030 and a modernised ePrescription system with fully digital certificates. The improvement is in strategy and in one service, as the integrated system and electronic health records are not yet in place.

A health digitalisation programme is adopted and ePrescription works, but the legal framework, the electronic health record and the national e-health entity are still planned, with the record due for 40% of the insured population by December 2027. The Government itself names the lack of a functional electronic health record, limited interoperability and no dedicated institutional framework as major challenges. What remains is a legal framework on eHealth aligned with the EU acquis, an interoperable integrated health information system and electronic health records in use.

Electronic health records for 40% of the insured population by December 2027 are a Reform Agenda payment condition, and the key recommendations on health in the 2024 and 2025 reports name an integrated e-health system, interoperability and digitalisation of health services. eHealth is a major digital public service within the theme, although no recommendation on it appears in the 2026 report among the 43 Moldova items on this issue.

The Government has adopted a programme and runs an ePrescription system that the Commission reports as modernised, which shows delivery capacity. The health record and interoperability need new legislation, a new institution, several health bodies and substantial funding in the Government's own estimates.

The 2022 Opinion found limited alignment with the EU electronic communications framework, and the 2023 report asked for alignment with the Electronic Communications Code and the Roaming Regulation. The 2024 report found that alignment had started and the 2025 report noted legislative advancements; in 2026 the Commission found the roaming acquis correctly transposed in full, the Code transposed in primary law with secondary legislation approximated, and the Gigabit Infrastructure Act reflected in a law adopted in June 2026. The Chapter 10 rating rates the whole chapter and was not decisive.

Law No. 72/2025, in force since January 2026, the roaming law and its secondary acts, and the 2026 infrastructure law respond to the requirements, and the Commission judged the related Reform Agenda step satisfactorily fulfilled. The regulator is still drafting secondary acts under the new law, an end-user protection regulation is planned for 2026, the Government plans to transpose the remaining electronic communications acts by the end of 2027, and a civil society monitor describes the new law as only partly compatible with the Code. What remains is completing and applying the secondary legislation under the Code and the Gigabit Infrastructure Act and transposing the remaining related acts.

Alignment with the roaming acquis and the Code was a key recommendation in the 2023, 2024 and 2025 reports and part of a Reform Agenda step, which would usually mean High. The Commission now finds the roaming acquis fully transposed and the step fulfilled, and no recommendation on this issue appears in the 2026 report among the 173 Moldova items on it, so the remaining work is narrower.

The main laws were adopted in 2025 and 2026 with EU technical support, and the Commission confirms the results, including entry into Roam Like at Home in January 2026. The remaining work is secondary legislation by one regulator and one ministry, which the regulator is already drafting.

The 2023 and 2024 reports call for more investment in infrastructure, including to overcome the rural-urban digital divide, and the 2025 Reform Agenda notes the absence of a comprehensive broadband mapping system. In 2026 the Commission found that the regulator's coverage platform and a new map of very high capacity networks provide relevant monitoring for investment decisions, while the 2026 report says that infrastructure investment remains well below needs. The issue spans several chapters, so chapter ratings were not decisive.

The mapping system is in operation, but the geographical survey of broadband coverage has a legal deadline of December 2030, the development of networks in white areas waits for it, and the state aid rules for broadband exist only as a draft. What remains is a national investment framework, with state aid rules and funding, that brings broadband to rural and white areas in line with EU connectivity targets.

The broadband mapping system was a Reform Agenda step, now fulfilled, and the 2023 and 2024 key recommendations on competitiveness ask for infrastructure investment, but they name digital infrastructure alongside energy and transport. No key recommendation specific to broadband planning appears among the 63 Moldova items on this issue.

The mapping step was delivered by 2026 through data sharing among the regulator, the cadastre agency and operators, and a World Bank project is analysing financing models. Extending networks to small and isolated localities needs substantial investment, and the Government's own timetable for the coverage survey runs to 2030.

The 2023 and 2024 reports found Moldova not aligned with the acquis on geo-blocking, platform-to-business relations, the Digital Services Act and the Digital Markets Act, and the 2025 report still found no alignment on the first two and the Digital Markets Act while noting that work on the Digital Services Act had started. The 2026 report finds alignment on geo-blocking and platform-to-business relations partial, with additional legislation in force in 2026, and initial steps on the institutional framework for both Acts. The improvement is legal and partial only.

Two 2025 laws partly transpose the platform-to-business and geo-blocking regulations, although Government sources give conflicting law numbers for them, the Competition Council is designated for the first, and the e-Commerce Directive is broadly aligned. The digital services law is still being drafted, the Digital Markets Act mechanism needs an amendment to the competition law, no supervisory authority for digital services exists yet, and the Government notes missing enforcement rules under the platform-to-business regulation. What remains is a legal basis and enforcement capacity for the Digital Services Act and the Digital Markets Act, and full alignment on geo-blocking and platform-to-business relations.

The 2024 and 2025 key recommendations ask Moldova to adopt and implement digital services legislation, bundled with media legislation, and the 2026 report repeats the need in its body text on binding acquis. Among the 86 Moldova items on this issue it is not named in a key recommendation in three reports, a benchmark or a Reform Agenda payment condition.

Two laws were adopted in 2025, and the Government plans to align with the Digital Services Act by the end of 2026, with EU4Digital experts helping on the draft. Enforcement needs new units in two regulators, while the ministry has one post for this area.
